sources.speaker: Tad Friend (author); Sam Altman, Paul Graham, Jack Altman, Connie Gibstine, Peter Thiel, Madelyn Gray and an unnamed YC stalwart quoted
sources.locator: Full text opened via curl (no paywall in HTML). Web date 2016-10-03, print issue 2016-10-10. Passages in order: Asperger's paragraph; prepper scene at a YC party; mother/Thiel paragraph; childhood and coming-out paragraph; Loopt paragraph (Graham 'powerful'); YC hand-off smile; brothers' dinner (Samurai); Team Human/melancholy; YC stalwart; managing; closing 'missing circuit' paragraph
sources.excerpt: “I was, like, ‘Fuck you, I don’t have Asperger’s!’ But then I thought, I can see why he thinks I do. I sit in weird ways”—he folds up like a busted umbrella—“I have narrow interests in technology, I have no patience for things I’m not interested in: parties, most people. When someone examines a photo and says, ‘Oh, he’s feeling this and this and this,’ all these subtle emotions, I look on with alien intrigue.” / His great weakness is his utter lack of interest in ineffective people, which unfortunately includes most of us. / “I try not to think about it too much,” Altman said. “But I have guns, gold, potassium iodide, antibiotics, batteries, water, gas masks from the Israeli Defense Force, and a big patch of land in Big Sur I can fly to.” / Altman’s mother, a dermatologist named Connie Gibstine, told me, “Sam does keep an awful lot tied up inside. He’ll call and say he has a headache—and he’ll have Googled it, so there’s some cyber-chondria in there, too. I have to reassure him that he doesn’t have meningitis or lymphoma, that it’s just stress.” / Thiel told me, “Sam is not particularly religious, but he is culturally very Jewish—an optimist yet a survivalist, with a sense that things can always go deeply wrong, and that there’s no single place in the world where you’re deeply at home.” / “Growing up gay in the Midwest in the two-thousands was not the most awesome thing,” he told me. “And finding AOL chat rooms was transformative. Secrets are bad when you’re eleven or twelve.” / After a Christian group boycotted an assembly about sexuality at his prep school, John Burroughs, Altman addressed the whole community, announcing that he was gay and asking whether the school wanted to be a repressive place or one open to different ideas. Madelyn Gray, Altman’s college counsellor, said, “What Sam did changed the school. It felt like someone had opened up a great big box full of all kinds of kids and let them out into the world.” / He was a formidable operator: quick to smile, but also quick to anger. If you cross him, he’ll joke about slipping ice-nine into your food. / Paul Graham, noting Altman’s early aura of consequence, told me, “Sam is extremely good at becoming powerful.” / Graham said, “I asked Sam in our kitchen, ‘Do you want to take over YC?,’ and he smiled, like, it worked. I had never seen an uncontrolled smile from Sam. It was like when you throw a ball of paper into the wastebasket across the room—that smile.” / Jack eyed a board game called Samurai on the bookshelf and said, “Sam won every single game of Samurai when we were kids because he always declared himself the Samurai leader: ‘I have to win, and I’m in charge of everything.’ ” / “I’m on Team Human. I don’t have a good logical reason why I’m sad, except that the class of things that humans are better at continues to narrow.” After a moment, he added, “ ‘Melancholy’ is a better word than ‘sad.’ ” / One YC stalwart told me, “Sam’s a little too focussed on glory—he puts his personal brand way out front. Under P.G., we had a family feel, and now it’s all institutional and aloof. Sam’s always managing up, but as the leader of the organization he needs to manage down.” / “I absolutely could do a better job at managing the organization—it was my chief weakness at Loopt, and I still have some learned helplessness about it. I don’t want to do weekly one-on-ones and let’s-talk-about-your-career-paths.” / “The missing circuit in my brain, the circuit that would make me care what people think about me, is a real gift. Most people want to be accepted, so they won’t take risks that could make them look crazy—which actually makes them wildly miscalculate risk.”
sources.context: Long profile based on extended in-person reporting with Altman, his family, Graham and Thiel. Altman's quoted lines were said directly to Friend; the 'great weakness', boycott and 'formidable operator' lines are Friend's narration. The YC stalwart is anonymous. This is the original source for Jack's Samurai line, the counsellor quote, the Christian-group boycott, the Graham kitchen smile (later re-quoted by The New Yorker in 2026) and the prepper list. Altman later said the prepper reputation had been 'caricatured very wildly' (S09). The 'missing circuit' self-report conflicts with his 2019 statements (S11, S13).

sources.excerpt: I am willing to take as much time as needed between projects to find my next thing. But I always want it to be a project that, if successful, will make the rest of my career look like a footnote. / Self-belief is immensely powerful. The most successful people I know believe in themselves almost to the point of delusion. / And unfortunately, the more ambitious you are, the more the world will try to tear you down. / Self-belief must be balanced with self-awareness. claims.claim: In 'A Fundraising Survival Guide' (August 2008), under the heading '5. Be independent.', Paul Graham wrote that when YC ('we') predicts good outcomes for startups, 'the qualities that come up in the supporting arguments are toughness, adaptability, determination', then: 'Sam Altman has it. You could parachute him into an island full of cannibals and come back in 5 years and he'd be the king.' Altman, born April 1985, was 23.
claims.passage: You could parachute him into an island full of cannibals and come back in 5 years and he'd be the king
claims.inference: A mentor-investor praising independence: a founder who can take care of himself and end up on top anywhere. The essay says nothing about reading rooms; the profile's link to room-winning is marked as its own reading (C94).
claims.alternative: Graham was praising a portfolio founder in a fundraising essay, so it is partly promotional. 'It' refers to the quality of not needing investors, not to accommodation.

claims.claim: In a blog post published on April 10, 2026, days after The New Yorker's investigation into whether he can be trusted (which the post calls 'an incendiary article about me a few days ago') and the night of the Molotov attack on his home, Altman wrote that he was proud of how he 'held the line' against Musk's bid for unilateral control, then: 'I am not proud of being conflict-averse, which has caused great pain for me and OpenAI.' The same post apologizes to 'people I've hurt'.
claims.passage: I am not proud of being conflict-averse, which has caused great pain for me and OpenAI
claims.inference: His own admission that conflict avoidance is a costly flaw. Because he offered it while answering charges of dishonesty, the profile treats it as his framing of disputed behavior (C124), not as an independent witness.
claims.alternative: 'Conflict-averse' is the most sympathetic available label for conduct board members call lying (C39, C119). The post was written under acute stress after an attack on his home. Conflict avoidance is also central to Type 9 and common in 2.

claims.claim: On April 10, 2026 a Molotov cocktail was thrown at Altman's home; a suspect was arrested and no one was hurt. Altman's blog post that night responds to the attack and to the New Yorker article.
claims.passage: the day someone threw a Molotov cocktail at his home
claims.inference: Dates the blog post the hook quotes. The draft gives no address or location detail beyond 'his home', does not name or characterize the suspect, and does not use anything he wrote about the attack as type evidence. One phrase from the post ('awake in the middle of the night and pissed') appears only as evidence that he feels anger in the moment, with the attack named as its context.
claims.alternative: A frightening attack; anger is an ordinary response under threat. Do not publish address details.

claims.claim: Graham's 2008 praise of an independent founder who can win any island and Altman's 2026 admission of conflict aversion describe one capacity from opposite ends. In this profile's reading, not Graham's, that capacity is persuasion: The New Yorker's 'ability to convince disparate groups that what he wants and what they need are one and the same', whose cost his biographer describes as telling people what they want to hear.
claims.passage: Read side by side, the two lines describe one capacity from opposite ends.
claims.inference: The profile's central frame, explicitly marked as the author's reading. It links Graham's 'deal-making ability' (C103) and the New Yorker's 'greatest strength' line (C105) to the self-reported and biographer-reported flaw (C41, C42).
claims.alternative: Graham was praising independence, close to the opposite of accommodation; adaptability and conflict aversion can be separate traits.

claims.claim: Samuel Harris Altman was born in Chicago on April 22, 1985.
claims.passage: Altman was born in Chicago on April 22, 1985.
claims.inference: Stable biographical frame; matches frontmatter birth_date (1985-04-22) and birth_place (Chicago). Re-checked in the Wikipedia Early life section on 2026-10-05.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is tertiary; if a primary record conflicts, use the birth year only.

claims.claim: Altman has been OpenAI's CEO since 2019, apart from five days in November 2023, and still held the title as of October 4, 2026.
claims.passage: he still held the job in early October 2026
claims.inference: Current-role check.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check on any leadership change or IPO; update the bio sentence, the description ('OpenAI's co-founder') and the 'OpenAI CEO' keyword together.

claims.claim: Leading type answer: Altman most likely fits Type 3 at medium confidence, with Type 4 as the strongest alternative and Type 8 as a serious second. The answer rests on colleagues' and his biographer's accounts of him adjusting to win each room while steering it toward his own aims, and on his own description of conflict aversion as a flaw that 'caused great pain'.
claims.passage: Sam Altman most likely fits Enneagram Type 3, the Achiever, at medium confidence.
claims.inference: Mirrors type_hypothesis (type 3, medium confidence, alternative 4). Confidence is stated in the answer, the FAQ and the meta title ('The Case for').
claims.alternative: See type_hypothesis.against and alternative_case. Much of the colleague testimony is anonymous or adversarial, and a salesman-CEO's incentives explain part of the pattern (C125).

claims.claim: Earlier versions of this page typed Altman as a 4w3 sp/so; the edited page ranks Four second. Several lines the old argument relied on were misquoted or unsourced and are not repeated: 'shameful' is one item in a run-on list (S84); the 'heart pounding, just terrified' quote is not in the cited episode (S85) and appears only in an anonymous compilation (S99); 'You should be skeptical of any company calling for its own regulation' is not in the Senate record (S29); 'We needed a structure that didn't exist' was not found (S32 is the nearest, not his words); the Coogan lines are not on the cited page (S08); he did call the firing 'unfair' (S40); the Ozymandias remark is from Masters of Scale, not Tyler Cowen (S12).
claims.passage: Earlier versions of this page read Altman as a Type 4
claims.inference: One transparency sentence for returning readers that the thesis changed; the article no longer argues against the old page elsewhere.
claims.alternative: The thesis change rests on the corrected record plus the repeated accommodation pattern (C75), not on the corrections alone; a 4w3 reading remains the strongest alternative and is argued in the draft.

claims.claim: Altman grew up in Clayton, Missouri, an affluent suburb of St. Louis, as the eldest of four siblings.
claims.passage: Altman grew up in Clayton, Missouri, outside St. Louis, the eldest of four siblings
claims.inference: Stable biographical frame from The New Yorker (2026), consistent with Wikipedia (family moved to Clayton in 1989).
claims.alternative: None material; sibling names are omitted from the draft.

claims.claim: At dinner with his brothers in 2016, with The New Yorker's Tad Friend present, Jack Altman said: 'Sam won every single game of Samurai when we were kids because he always declared himself the Samurai leader: ‘I have to win, and I’m in charge of everything.’'
claims.passage: he always declared himself the Samurai leader: 'I have to win, and I'm in charge of everything'
claims.inference: A sibling's affectionate anecdote that shows early competitiveness and a wish to be in charge. It is consistent with the adult pattern of seeking the top role, but it is one board-game story told by a brother at a family dinner in front of a reporter.
claims.alternative: Childhood competitiveness is common to many types and to eldest siblings. The Common Reader (S05) recasts the line as Sam's general 'attitude'; quote the 2016 original with its Samurai context. The published page sources it to the Common Reader, which is secondhand.

claims.claim: At about 17, after a Christian group boycotted an assembly about sexuality at the John Burroughs School, Altman addressed the whole school and announced that he was gay (New Yorker, 2016). In 2020 he recalled rewriting the section where he told his own story 'back and forth like three times, because I just couldn't do it.'
claims.passage: back and forth like three times, because I just couldn't do it
claims.inference: A costly, voluntary act of public self-disclosure at 17. It is the strongest early evidence that he will risk social standing to state something true about himself. It fits the published Type 4 reading (claiming difference at cost) and also a values-driven courage that any type can show.
claims.alternative: He says he was already 'mostly out' and that most people knew. The ovation and the student reactions are his own recollection two decades later. NYMag and Wikipedia describe the trigger as objections to a National Coming Out Day speaker. A single adolescent act, well received, cannot carry a lifelong motive by itself.

claims.claim: The coming-out speech is the clearest early evidence that Altman will spend social standing to say something true about himself and to challenge an institution in public, and it is the Four reading's best exhibit, qualified by his statement that he was already 'mostly out'.
claims.passage: this is the clearest early evidence that he will spend social standing to say something true about himself
claims.inference: A costly, voluntary self-disclosure and a public challenge at 17. The draft labels it the strongest support for the Type 4 alternative and returns to it in 'What the type doesn't explain' as the open confrontation the conflict-averse thesis does not predict.
claims.alternative: He was 'mostly out' and most people knew; the act was well received. A single adolescent act cannot carry a lifelong motive, and values-driven courage is available to any type.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker (2026) that at sixteen or seventeen he was physically attacked and subjected to homophobic slurs in St. Louis. He declined to give more detail on the record.
claims.passage: at sixteen or seventeen he was physically attacked and called homophobic slurs in St. Louis
claims.inference: Biographical fact reported once, from his account only. The edited draft uses it only in the childhood section and nowhere as type evidence; his stated reason for withholding details is no longer quoted.
claims.alternative: Reticence about an assault is common and reflects privacy or self-protection. Sensitive personal material; add no detail beyond his account and no location beyond the city.

claims.claim: Altman offered a hedged guess about the attack's legacy: 'probably that has, like, some deep-seated psychological thing—that I think I’m over but I’m not—about not wanting more conflict.'
claims.passage: probably that has, like, some deep-seated psychological thing
claims.inference: This is the only causal childhood link in the draft, and it is his own hedged speculation ('probably'). The draft labels it as speculation and states that the profile builds nothing on it.
claims.alternative: Not established cause; conflict avoidance has many sources, including professional incentive (C42). Do not expand into a childhood-wound narrative.

claims.claim: Altman studied computer science at Stanford for two years, dropped out and co-founded Loopt, a location-based app, in 2005, at 19. Loopt was in Y Combinator's first batch, which is how Graham came to fund him.
claims.passage: Altman left Stanford after two years to co-found Loopt, a location-sharing app, in 2005, at 19.
claims.inference: Stable career facts.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is tertiary; the Stanford years and Loopt date were re-checked in the article text on 2026-10-05.

claims.claim: Graham told The New Yorker in 2016: 'Sam is extremely good at becoming powerful.'
claims.passage: Sam is extremely good at becoming powerful
claims.inference: A mentor's direct characterization centered on acquiring power and position, used as an Eight exhibit.
claims.alternative: It describes skill, not motive. An 8 seeks power to avoid being controlled; a 3 acquires it as success and status. The quote cannot separate those.

claims.claim: According to Keach Hagey's biography as reported by The New Yorker (2026), senior Loopt employees 'concerned with Altman's leadership and lack of transparency' twice asked the board to fire him. Mark Jacobstein, an older employee, told Hagey: 'There's a blurring between 'I think I can maybe accomplish this thing' and 'I have already accomplished this thing' that in its most toxic form leads to Theranos.' A board member denied that the attempts to remove Altman were serious.
claims.passage: There's a blurring between 'I think I can maybe accomplish this thing' and 'I have already accomplished this thing' that in its most toxic form leads to Theranos
claims.inference: This is the earliest professional evidence, from his early twenties and before OpenAI's stakes. It shows the same pattern later reported at OpenAI: an inflated presentation that blurs aspiration and accomplishment, and leadership opacity. Jacobstein's 'blurring' describes self-deception in favor of an achieving self-image, a classic Type 3 marker.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia notes Altman's supporters said the attempts 'were not serious'. Exaggeration is a common founder sales habit with a professional incentive (raising money for a pre-product startup; Emmett Shear's 'convincing phone companies to give his startup ... deals', S08). The sources are secondhand through Hagey.

claims.claim: Karen Hao's Empire of AI (pp. 34-35), as quoted in a critic's compilation, cites an unnamed person who worked with Altman for several years in the Loopt era: 'He's so attentive. But then part of it is he uses that to figure out how to influence you in different ways. He's so good at adjusting to what you say, and you really feel like you're making progress with him.'
claims.passage: He's so good at adjusting to what you say, and you really feel like you're making progress with him
claims.inference: Describes adaptive mirroring and attentiveness used for influence, at Loopt, years before OpenAI. The influence clause (cut in the earlier draft) is what separates this from a Two's attentiveness and reconciles it with his low-EQ self-reports (C108).
claims.alternative: Verified only via a critic's compilation of the book (S55), which the link text names; anonymous. Attentiveness also fits Type 2.

claims.claim: In March 2012, after failing to gain significant user traction, Loopt was acquired by Green Dot for $43.4 million.
claims.passage: Loopt sold for $43.4 million
claims.inference: Stable career fact.
claims.alternative: Tertiary source; re-checked 2026-10-05.

claims.claim: Jacobstein's 'blurring' between aspiration and accomplishment describes someone who comes to believe the version of himself that wins the room; that self-deception, more than plain lying, is the classic Type 3 trap, and Sue Yoon described something similar years later.
claims.passage: That kind of self-deception, more than plain lying, is the classic Type 3 trap
claims.inference: Connects two named accounts (Jacobstein via Hagey, Yoon on the record) from different decades to the Type 3 passion of deceit as identification with the image.
claims.alternative: The draft first offers the generous reading (a pre-product company must sell what it will become). Exaggeration is a common founder sales habit, and both accounts are reported secondhand through journalists.

claims.claim: Altman succeeded Graham as YC president in 2014. Graham told The New Yorker in 2016 that when he offered Altman the job in his kitchen, 'he smiled, like, it worked. I had never seen an uncontrolled smile from Sam.'
claims.passage: he smiled, like, it worked. I had never seen an uncontrolled smile from Sam.
claims.inference: Graham's word 'uncontrolled' implies that Altman's usual face was controlled; what slipped through was the pleasure of a won goal.
claims.alternative: One moment, read through a mentor's metaphor. It is equally a sign of a goal achieved. The original source is the 2016 article; the 2026 piece re-quotes it.

claims.claim: Karen Hao reports (Empire of AI, p. 42, in a passage the critic's compilation places in Altman's YC years): 'In private settings and with close friends, he still showed flashes of anger and frustration. In public ones and with acquaintances, he embodied the nice guy.' After an elision the compilation marks, the passage continues that he 'avoided expressing negative emotions, avoided confrontation, avoided saying no to people.'
claims.passage: avoided expressing negative emotions, avoided confrontation, avoided saying no to people
claims.inference: Hao describes a public self managed to a role, with private anger. The edited draft marks the elision, drops the unsupported 'new president' framing, names the compilation, says the context could not be checked against the book, and uses the passage only alongside independent evidence of the public/private split (C98, C131).
claims.alternative: The book was not opened directly; the text was verified only through a critic's compilation (S55). Executive self-presentation coaching is common.

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman told The New Yorker, while waving off a suggestion that he had Asperger's: 'When someone examines a photo and says, 'Oh, he's feeling this and this and this,' all these subtle emotions, I look on with alien intrigue.'
claims.passage: all these subtle emotions, I look on with alien intrigue.
claims.inference: A self-report about reading other people's emotions, not about his own feelings. The edited draft presents it that way and no longer uses it as evidence that he brackets his own feeling.
claims.alternative: Said while joking off an Asperger's suggestion, partly as self-deprecating humor. It sits beside colleagues' accounts of uncanny attentiveness (C44); the profile reconciles the two in C108 rather than counting either for Three.

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman told The New Yorker: 'The missing circuit in my brain, the circuit that would make me care what people think about me, is a real gift. Most people want to be accepted, so they won't take risks that could make them look crazy—which actually makes them wildly miscalculate risk.' The draft quotes the first two sentences.
claims.passage: The missing circuit in my brain, the circuit that would make me care what people think about me, is a real gift.
claims.inference: A first-person denial of the approval motive at Type 3's core, framed around risk-taking. The edited draft presents it as counterevidence in 'What the type doesn't explain' and names the observation that would weaken the Three reading (risks that cost approval outside fights over control).
claims.alternative: His January 2019 remark to Tyler Cowen (C86) qualifies it. A Type 8 or 5 could sincerely report not caring; the 2016 line is about risk, not all approval.

claims.claim: In a January 2019 Conversations with Tyler taping Altman said: 'And all of us, myself included, are much more affected by what other people think of us and our ideas than we like to admit.'
claims.passage: all of us, myself included, are much more affected by what other people think of us and our ideas than we like to admit
claims.inference: Partly qualifies his 2016 'missing circuit' claim (C22). The draft says it qualifies the boast without turning it into support for Three.
claims.alternative: Self-understanding changes; the 2016 line concerned risk-taking, and the 2019 line is a general remark about people.

claims.claim: On November 17, 2023, while Altman was in Las Vegas for a Formula 1 race, the OpenAI board fired him on a video call. Its statement said he 'was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities.' The draft and the firing FAQ quote the first clause.
claims.passage: Altman was in Las Vegas for a Formula 1 race when the board fired him on a video call
claims.inference: The documented event that anchors the firing section.
claims.alternative: The board's statement gave no specifics. WilmerHale later found the board acted within its discretion but that his conduct 'did not mandate removal' (C50).

claims.claim: That night Altman posted: 'i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you’re still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are.'
claims.passage: sorta like reading your own eulogy while you're still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome
claims.inference: His public response reframes rejection as an outpouring of love, a positive public face within hours. It shows reception-focused framing: how others see him is the experience he reports.
claims.alternative: Gratitude in the moment is also a genuine human response, and a strategic one: the public campaign for his return began that night (S43). Quote the lowercase originals in full.

claims.claim: After the firing Altman set up what he called a 'sort of government-in-exile' at his house, where advisers including Airbnb's Brian Chesky and the crisis-communications manager Chris Lehane built a public case for his return.
claims.passage: he set up what he called a "sort of government-in-exile,"
claims.inference: The response to threat included an organized public campaign. The draft says only 'at home' and gives no property or location detail.
claims.alternative: Any executive fighting a sudden firing would assemble advisers; Lehane's role reflects the stakes as much as Altman's personality.

claims.claim: In January 2025 Altman told Bloomberg that when two board members called about his return he was 'initially just supermad and said no', then set a condition: 'Only if the whole board quits.' He added: 'I wish I had taken a different tack than that, but at the time it felt like a just thing to ask for.'
claims.passage: I was initially just supermad and said no.
claims.inference: He reports anger in the moment and a hard power demand when control of the company was at stake, which supports the Type 8 alternative and the draft's point that he confronts openly when control is on the line. It also shows real-time feeling, which is why the draft no longer claims his feelings arrive only later.
claims.alternative: Ordinary anger at a firing; reported retrospectively in a controlled interview, with his own later regret about the demand (C115).

claims.claim: Within days, 745 of OpenAI's 770 employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless the board resigned. After pressure from employees and investors, Altman was reinstated within five days of the firing.
claims.passage: 745 of OpenAI's 770 employees signed a letter threatening to quit unless the board resigned
claims.inference: Documented. The employee rally shows deep loyalty among staff, a real counterweight to the critics' testimony, and it was a large part of the leverage behind his return (C97).
claims.alternative: Employees also had financial stakes and a Microsoft exit option (C114), so the letter mixes loyalty with incentives. Reinstatement is dated November 21 or 22 in different sources; the draft says only 'within five days'.

claims.claim: In a tense call after the firing, as the board pressed him to acknowledge a pattern of deception, Altman said 'This is just so fucked up' repeatedly and also 'I can't change my personality', according to people on the call. Altman says he does not recall the exchange; he said 'It's possible I meant something like 'I do try to be a unifying force,'' added that the trait had enabled him to lead an immensely successful company, and attributed the criticism to a tendency, especially early in his career, 'to be too much of a conflict avoider'. A board member said: 'What it meant was 'I have this trait where I lie to people, and I'm not going to stop.''
claims.passage: I can't change my personality.
claims.inference: Whatever he meant, his own gloss links the trait to unifying people and avoiding conflict, not to an inner identity. That is evidence for accommodation, not Type 4 self-definition.
claims.alternative: Contested on every side: anonymous recall, his non-recollection, opposing interpretations. Only 'This is just so fucked up' is described as repeated, and the draft says so. The New Yorker dates the call only as after the firing.

claims.claim: On Lex Fridman's podcast (March 2024), about four months after the firing, Altman called it 'definitely the most painful professional experience of my life, and chaotic and shameful and upsetting and a bunch of other negative things.'
claims.passage: definitely the most painful professional experience of my life, and chaotic and shameful and upsetting and a bunch of other negative things
claims.inference: He names shame among several negative feelings. The published page's central 'shameful' argument rests on this one word, but it is a single adjective in a run-on list, not a chosen standalone word. It cannot discriminate Type 4 from Type 3: shame is the heart-triad emotion for 2, 3 and 4, and public firing triggers it in most people.
claims.alternative: The published page renders it as 'Chaotic. And shameful. And upsetting.' and builds a section on 'the word that stayed'. Quote the clause as spoken.

claims.claim: A Four reading leans on the word 'shameful', which is one item in a run-on list of negative feelings; a public firing would shame most people, so the word cannot discriminate Type 4 from Type 3.
claims.passage: A Four reading leans on "shameful," but it is one item in a run-on list, and a public firing would shame most people.
claims.inference: Corrects the published page's central misquote and addresses the Type 4 hypothesis directly rather than the old page.
claims.alternative: Shame is the heart-triad emotion for 2, 3 and 4; his naming it at all is mild support for a heart-triad core.

claims.claim: During the firing weekend Altman ran a public campaign (advisers, a public case, a post that turned rejection into an 'outpouring of love'), but much of the leverage behind his return came from others: Brockman's resignation, Microsoft's announced job offer, investors and the employee letter.
claims.passage: The campaign was his; the leverage was mostly other people's.
claims.inference: Separates what the episode shows about Altman (an image-focused campaign) from the structural leverage that forced the board's hand, so the campaign is not over-credited as personal will.
claims.alternative: The New Yorker reports Altman coordinating closely with Nadella, so the Microsoft offer was not wholly others' doing. Campaign-building after a sudden firing is common to any executive.

claims.claim: 'Artificial', Luca Guadagnino's biographical comedy-drama about the November 2023 firing, written by Simon Rich and starring Andrew Garfield as Altman, was scheduled to premiere at the New York Film Festival on October 5, 2026, with a U.S. release from Neon set for December 25, 2026. The film is a dramatization and is not evidence about his psychology.
claims.passage: scheduled to premiere at the New York Film Festival on October 5, 2026
claims.inference: Current context that explains renewed search interest; the draft and FAQ state that it is not used as evidence.
claims.alternative: Release details may change (limited vs wide release is unconfirmed). Reviews and the film's accuracy are unknown as of 2026-10-05. The published page's line that he cannot rule this 'island' is speculative; he has now commented publicly.
claims.review_trigger: After the Oct 5, 2026 NYFF premiere and the Dec 25, 2026 release, confirm both happened as scheduled and restate them in the past tense (body and FAQ); re-check reception and any further Altman comment; never cite the film as evidence of motive.

claims.claim: Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI co-founder and then its chief scientist, wrote 2023 memos to the board; one about Altman begins with a list headed 'Sam exhibits a consistent pattern of . . .' whose first item is 'Lying', and in one he seemed concerned about entrusting the technology to someone who 'just tells people what they want to hear'. In a 2025 deposition he called the process 'rushed' and said much of the material came from Mira Murati, interim CEO during the crisis, and that he knew it 'through secondhand knowledge'. Murati told The New Yorker: 'Everything I shared was accurate, and I stand behind all of it.'
claims.passage: Sam exhibits a consistent pattern of . . .
claims.inference: Another independent use of 'tells people what they want to hear' (2023), by a co-founder.
claims.alternative: Secondhand and contested; the memo itself was not produced. Sutskever publicly regretted the board's action days later and signed the employee letter (C117), without retracting the memos. Do not present 'consistent pattern of lying' as established.

claims.claim: Helen Toner, one of the four directors who fired Altman, said on the TED AI Show (May 28, 2024) that 'for years, Sam had made it really difficult for the board to actually do that job by, you know, withholding information'. OpenAI's response, via board chair Bret Taylor, said it was 'disappointed that Ms. Toner continues to revisit these issues.' Altman told Bloomberg in January 2025: 'I don't think I was doing things that were sneaky.'
claims.passage: made the board's job "really difficult" by "withholding information"
claims.inference: First-person testimony from a board member who voted to fire him. It is consistent in kind with C41-C46: managing information and others' impressions to keep control without open conflict.
claims.alternative: Toner is an interested party. OpenAI and the WilmerHale summary dispute the framing. The draft quotes Toner's words from the TED transcript as partial quotes and gives both responses.

claims.claim: OpenAI's summary of the WilmerHale review (March 8, 2024) found that the prior board 'acted within its broad discretion' to terminate Altman but that 'his conduct did not mandate removal.' No written report was released.
claims.passage: his conduct did not mandate removal
claims.inference: Documented outcome: neither exoneration of the candor concerns nor a finding that removal was required.
claims.alternative: Written by the post-reinstatement board; the New Yorker reports the findings were oral briefings only.

claims.claim: Keach Hagey, author of the biography 'The Optimist' (2025), who interviewed Altman several times, said: 'he is not great at dealing with conflict, so he'll basically tell people what they want to hear. That causes a lot of sturm und drang in the management ranks, and it's a pattern.' Of his trust problems: 'This happened both at his first startup and very famously at OpenAI, as well as at Y Combinator. So it is a pattern, but I think it's a typical critique of people who have the salesman skill set.'
claims.passage: not great at dealing with conflict, so he'll basically tell people what they want to hear
claims.inference: A biographer with direct access names one pattern across three organizations and two decades: telling people what they want to hear to avoid conflict. Repetition across contexts and time is what the standard asks for. It favors an approval-adaptive motive (3, or 9/2) over a 4 who protects emotional authenticity.
claims.alternative: Hagey explicitly offers the incentive explanation: 'a typical critique of people who have the salesman skill set'. A fundraiser-CEO's job rewards telling each audience what it wants. The pattern could be learned practice rather than core motive, although it predates OpenAI's stakes.

claims.claim: Karen Hao reported in The Atlantic (May 2025) that 'Many of Altman’s closest executives had long observed a particular pattern in his behavior: If two teams disagreed, he often agreed in private with each of their perspectives, which created confusion and bred mistrust among colleagues.'
claims.passage: he often agreed in private with each of their perspectives
claims.inference: A concrete behavioral form of accommodation in the room: agreement mirrors whoever is present. Cited at the start of 'Why Type 3 leads'.
claims.alternative: Anonymous sources. A CEO keeping factions on board may be deliberate management, not a need for approval. 'Telling people what they want to hear' does not appear literally in the Atlantic excerpt.

claims.claim: An unnamed board member told The New Yorker (2026) that Altman has 'two traits that are almost never seen in the same person. The first is a strong desire to please people, to be liked in any given interaction. The second is almost a sociopathic lack of concern for the consequences that may come from deceiving someone.'
claims.passage: a strong desire to please people, to be liked in any given interaction
claims.inference: The board member's first trait, 'a strong desire to please people, to be liked in any given interaction', is a close lay description of the Type 3 pattern of shaping the presented self to what wins approval in each room. Joined to a sustained will to power and to deception, it is also the core of the critics' case.
claims.alternative: An anonymous, adversarial characterization by someone involved in the firing. 'Sociopathic' is a pejorative, not a diagnosis; the draft says so explicitly. A desire to be liked also fits Types 2 and 9.

claims.claim: Former OpenAI board member Sue Yoon told The New Yorker (2026) that Altman was 'not this Machiavellian villain' but able, to the point of 'fecklessness', to convince himself of the shifting realities of his sales pitches: 'He’s too caught up in his own self-belief.'
claims.passage: He's too caught up in his own self-belief.
claims.inference: A named, relatively sympathetic insider describes self-deception: he believes his own pitch. That is the Type 3 passion (deceit as identification with the image) more precisely than lying, and it matches Jacobstein's 'blurring' at Loopt (C14).
claims.alternative: Named but brief. The published page claims Yoon 'ended up describing a Type 4'; nothing in her words is specific to 4.

claims.claim: Altman's April 2026 post called the New Yorker investigation 'an incendiary article'. Ronan Farrow, its co-author, said it 'was meticulously fact-checked, and OpenAI is not disputing the core facts.'
claims.passage: OpenAI is not disputing the core facts
claims.inference: Context for weighing the New Yorker's testimony: Altman rejects its framing, and its author says its core facts are not disputed.
claims.alternative: Both statements are self-interested.

claims.claim: Across three organizations and two decades, sources describe one recurring behavior: in the room, Altman accommodates the person or faction in front of him rather than risk a fight (telling people what they want to hear, agreeing privately with each side, adjusting to what you say, avoiding saying no); outside the room, he pursues his own aims indirectly (trying to get board members off the board; pressing the product side to keep going while sympathizing with safety). Sources include Loopt colleagues (via Hao and Hagey), YC partners (via The New Yorker and Hagey), co-founders in 2017, board members and executives in 2023, Toner in 2024, and his biographer in 2025. Altman names the trait himself as conflict aversion, mostly while answering charges of dishonesty.
claims.passage: Altman accommodates whoever is in front of him rather than risk a fight
claims.inference: This is the strongest repeated, costly, cross-context pattern in the record. It cost him two removal attempts at Loopt, YC partners' trust and the 2023 firing. The motive it best fits is keeping a winning, approved image in each interaction while pursuing his own direction: Type 3's adaptation of the presented self. A core 4 typically protects authentic self-expression even at the cost of approval; an 8 fights in the open.
claims.alternative: Professional incentive is the main rival explanation (C125). Much of the testimony is anonymous or adversarial. Type 9 and Type 2 also explain accommodation; the agenda that survives the accommodation (C127) separates 3 from them.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker (2026) that his main flaw as a manager had been his eagerness to avoid conflict, and: 'Now I'm very happy to fire people quickly.'
claims.passage: Now I'm very happy to fire people quickly
claims.inference: His own claim that the defining pattern has changed. The draft marks it as a self-assessment, not yet a record, and ties it to the closing forward test.
claims.alternative: A CEO's self-description in a hostile investigation; the change is asserted, not shown.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check at the next major profile and by 2027-10-05: look for named colleague or board testimony after April 2026 describing him delivering unwelcome decisions directly, or a public position he holds at a real cost in approval outside a fight over control. Update the closing paragraph and the conflict-averse FAQ either way.

claims.claim: In the 'Honest Thoughts' email of September 20, 2017, written during negotiations over control of OpenAI and signed by Ilya Sutskever and Greg Brockman, they wrote to Altman: 'We don't understand why the CEO title is so important to you. Your stated reasons have changed, and it's hard to really understand what's driving it.'
claims.passage: We don't understand why the CEO title is so important to you.
claims.inference: Contemporaneous co-founders, six years before the firing, puzzled that the top title mattered so much and that his stated reasons shifted. Title importance plus shifting rationales fits a status-oriented self that adapts its explanations. The same email credits him with firmness against Musk, which complicates a pure conflict-avoider picture.
claims.alternative: Written during a high-stakes negotiation over control; co-founders had their own interests. Litigation release via a third-party compilation; court PDF not opened.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker (2026): 'I’m very ambitious as far as, like, my hope for humanity, and what I expect us all to achieve. I weirdly have very little personal ambition.' He then added: 'No one believes you’re doing this just because it’s interesting ... You’re doing it for power or for some other thing.'
claims.passage: I weirdly have very little personal ambition
claims.inference: Counterevidence to a status-driven reading. The draft presents both halves of his distinction, does not treat the denial as support for Three, says he may experience the drive as mission, and names the observation that would separate the readings: whether he ever gives up the top role or a public win because the mission requires it.
claims.alternative: He may mean it. The New Yorker notes that even people close to him cannot tell where 'hope for humanity' ends and ambition begins.

claims.claim: The drive in the record aims at a specific prize, the top title: in September 2017 Sutskever and Brockman wrote to Altman that they did not understand 'why the CEO title is so important to you', adding 'Your stated reasons have changed'. Power-seeking alone cannot separate Type 3 from Type 8.
claims.passage: The prize is the top job.
claims.inference: Title and visible standing are the Three-specific part of the drive; the draft states that power-seeking alone does not separate 3 from 8 and hands that question to the Eight section.
claims.alternative: Ambition is required by his roles and is not type-specific. He may experience the drive as mission (C30). Co-founders writing during a negotiation had their own interests.

claims.claim: In January 2025 Altman told Bloomberg, discussing how much tension he had detected on OpenAI's board before the firing: 'I don't think I'm a person with a strong EQ at all, but even for me this was over the line of where I could detect that there was tension' and 'I'm not a high-EQ person, so there's probably even more.'
claims.passage: I'm not a high-EQ person
claims.inference: A second self-report about reading others, given while discussing how much board tension he had sensed. Not used as evidence about his own feelings.
claims.alternative: Doubles as an explanation for underestimating the board; self-reported EQ is a weak measure. Conflicts with colleagues' accounts of attentiveness used for influence (C44), which C108 addresses.

claims.claim: In October 2016 Altman wrote that 'Donald Trump represents an unprecedented threat to America'. On January 21, 2025, at the White House announcement of the Stargate AI-infrastructure project, he said: 'We wouldn’t be able to do this without you, Mr. President.' On January 22 he posted: 'watching @potus more carefully recently has really changed my perspective on him (i wish i had done more of my own thinking and definitely fell in the npc trap).'
claims.passage: i wish i had done more of my own thinking and definitely fell in the npc trap
claims.inference: A documented reversal toward the person in power, recast as independent thinking ('npc trap'). The appeal to independence has a distinctiveness (Four-like) flavor, which the draft acknowledges; what fits Three is that the claim of independence was used to present a move toward power.
claims.alternative: Many executives courted the new administration for corporate reasons; this may be business pragmatism rather than a type motive. The draft states that alternative.

claims.claim: Where looking credible and looking distinctive pull apart, Altman's choices favor credibility: he framed his equity regret around 'conspiracy theories' (2025), giving up his most distinctive status marker for credibility, and he recast his Trump reversal as escaping 'the npc trap' (2025).
claims.passage: What he guards is an image of being credible, effective and likeable
claims.inference: Combined with C75 and C76, this favors 3 over 4 because the attention goes to appearing credible, effective and likeable rather than distinctive. The edited draft removed two earlier exhibits (assault reticence; 'words and narratives' after the attack) whose context did not support an image motive.
claims.alternative: Any public figure under intense scrutiny manages perception. This is an interpretive pattern, not proof of motive.

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman told The New Yorker: 'I'm on Team Human. I don't have a good logical reason why I'm sad, except that the class of things that humans are better at continues to narrow.' After a moment: ''Melancholy' is a better word than 'sad.'' The draft paraphrases the first part and quotes the correction.
claims.passage: 'Melancholy' is a better word than 'sad.'
claims.inference: His own choice of 'melancholy' about humanity's narrowing advantage is a 4-flavored word. It is the best single piece of support for a 4 or 4-wing coloring in his vocabulary.
claims.alternative: It concerns AI's trajectory, not his self. It is one remark.

claims.claim: In an email to Elon Musk on February 18, 2023 Altman wrote: 'well, you’re my hero and that’s what it feels like when you attack openai. i am tremendously thankful for everything you’ve done to help–i don’t think openai would have happened without you–and it really fucking hurts when you publicly attack openai.' Musk replied that it was 'certainly not my intention to be hurtful'.
claims.passage: it really fucking hurts when you publicly attack openai
claims.inference: A private, direct expression of hurt to an adversary. It is the strongest evidence that he does voice feeling in conflict, and it supports the published Type 4 reading's 'vulnerability first'. It is also a relational appeal (a 2-like move) that seeks to repair the relationship by naming admiration and hurt.
claims.alternative: Written privately to a powerful co-founder and funder whose attacks threatened OpenAI; it may be strategic as well as sincere. It was an email, not a text, and is all lowercase.

claims.claim: In December 2024 Altman told Bari Weiss that Musk is 'also clearly a bully'.
claims.passage: In public he called Musk "clearly a bully"
claims.inference: He pairs criticism with praise and depersonalizes the conflict as a pattern in Musk. This is a measured public posture that keeps him likeable and makes Musk the aggressor.
claims.alternative: The same answer praises Musk as 'a sort of legendary entrepreneur' and is prefaced as speculation; the draft quotes only the two words.

claims.claim: When Musk led a $97.4 billion bid for OpenAI's controlling nonprofit, Altman posted on February 10, 2025: 'no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want'.
claims.passage: no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want
claims.inference: Public jabs delivered as wit and pity. He wins the exchange without appearing aggressive.
claims.alternative: The published page reads the 'insecurity' remark as empathy. It can equally be a status move that frames the rival as pitiable. Use the corrected wording.

claims.claim: The private 2023 email to Musk is raw; the public lines about Musk win the exchange without making Altman look like the aggressor.
claims.passage: The email is raw; the public lines win the exchange without making him look like the aggressor.
claims.inference: Contrasts private hurt (the Four reading's best adult exhibit) with managed public positioning (consistent with Type 3 image management).
claims.alternative: Public wit about a litigious rival is ordinary media practice; the email itself was written to a powerful funder and may be partly strategic.

claims.claim: Altman's 2023 compensation from OpenAI was $76,001 (tax filing). As of May 2026 he held no direct OpenAI equity. In October 2025 he wrote: 'i do wish i had taken equity a long time ago and i think it would have led to far fewer conspiracy theories'.
claims.passage: His 2023 pay from OpenAI was $76,001
claims.inference: The no-equity arrangement is real but weaker evidence of anti-status motivation than the published page claims. It began as a governance constraint of the nonprofit structure. He is a billionaire through other holdings. He says he wishes he had taken equity, and frames that regret around public perception ('conspiracy theories'). That last point is evidence of image-awareness.
claims.alternative: The published page's 'Meaning Over Money' bullet and its present-tense '$76,001 ... no equity ... valued at over $300 billion' are outdated or incomplete. The 'childhood dream job' line still supports a sincere mission or interest motive, which fits any type.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if OpenAI grants Altman equity (The New Yorker reported in April 2026 that the arrangement could soon change), if a new Form 990 or IPO filing discloses pay, or if the S-1 becomes public.

claims.claim: In a 2024 Advocate Q&A Altman said: 'I don’t really think about being a gay CEO. I don’t look at it that way.'
claims.passage: I don't really think about being a gay CEO.
claims.inference: He plays down his sexuality as central to his self-concept, which weakens the old reading of the coming-out speech as the start of a lifelong identity project.
claims.alternative: A short answer in an edited Q&A; not discussing an identity is not the same as it lacking importance.

claims.claim: Each Type 4 exhibit has limits: he was already 'mostly out' before the speech and plays down his sexuality's place in his identity; 'melancholy' concerned humanity's prospects; and the Four's core motive, protecting an authentic self even when it costs approval, is hard to find in the adult record, though a reserved Four, or one with a strong Three wing, could look similar as a public CEO.
claims.passage: The Four's core motive, protecting an authentic self even when it costs approval, is hard to find in the adult record
claims.inference: States why Type 4 remains the live alternative but not the lead.
claims.alternative: The private Musk email (C51) and the speech (C07) are genuine costly or unguarded expressions; a 4w3 in a public role would show fewer of them.

claims.claim: A former OpenAI employee told The New Yorker (2026) that Altman once said: 'I don’t care about money. I care more about power.'
claims.passage: I don't care about money. I care more about power.
claims.inference: If accurate, it reframes the no-equity story: money is not the currency, power is. That supports power/status drives (3 or 8) over the meaning-only reading.
claims.alternative: Anonymous recollection of an informal remark, not on the record. Altman says he is not primarily motivated by wealth. Use only with attribution to 'a former employee recalled', or omit.

claims.claim: In the same September 2017 email Sutskever and Brockman told Musk that 'Sam acted as a genuine counterbalance to you' and that in the negotiation they 'were ready to sweep the long-term AGI control questions under the rug while Sam stood his ground.'
claims.passage: Sam stood his ground
claims.inference: Contemporaneous evidence that Altman refused a powerful counterpart when control was at stake; supports the Type 8 alternative and complicates a pure conflict-avoider picture.
claims.alternative: Written during a high-stakes negotiation in which the authors had their own interests.

claims.claim: In his April 10, 2026 post Altman wrote that he was proud of how much he 'held the line on not being willing to agree to the unilateral control he wanted over OpenAI', referring to Musk.
claims.passage: held the line on not being willing to agree to the unilateral control
claims.inference: His own claim of firmness against Musk, quoted in the hook; supports the Type 8 alternative.
claims.alternative: Self-reported pride, written the same night as his admission of conflict aversion and ahead of the Musk trial.

claims.claim: Altman confronts openly when control of the institution is on the line (2017, 2023). Elsewhere he accommodates in the room and, when he moves against people, does it indirectly: trying to get board members off the board, by his own account, and misleading other directors to do it, by Toner's.
claims.passage: Altman confronts openly when control of the institution is on the line, as in 2017 and 2023.
claims.inference: The discriminator between 3 and 8: an Eight tends to fight in the open; sidelining opponents while keeping the public face clean fits a Three better.
claims.alternative: Two episodes of open confrontation are few; private anger (Hao; Friend's 'quick to anger') suggests more confrontation than the public record shows. Toner's account is disputed by OpenAI (C121).

claims.claim: Altman's sister Annie has said publicly since at least November 2021 that she experienced abuse from her siblings, mostly from Sam. In January 2025 she sued him in federal court in Missouri, alleging that he sexually abused her beginning when she was 3 and he was 12. Sam, their mother and their brothers Jack and Max said in a joint statement: 'All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.' The New Yorker 'could not substantiate Annie’s account.'
claims.passage: All of these claims are utterly untrue.
claims.inference: A grave, unresolved allegation that a responsible profile must acknowledge, with the denial and its unresolved status. It is not type evidence, and the draft says so. The draft does not repeat the family statement's characterizations of Annie's health or finances.
claims.alternative: Unadjudicated, contested, and involving mental-health characterizations in the family statement that should not be repeated as fact. The published page's 'The litigation is ongoing' remains accurate as of 2026-09-30, but the procedural posture has changed. Keep medical and IME details out of copy.

The Oct 2, 2026 hearing has passed; no outcome was on the docket as of 2026-10-05 (latest entry #128, Sept 30).

claims.claim: On March 20, 2026 the court dismissed Annie Altman's common-law claims as time-barred and allowed an amended complaint, which she filed on April 1, 2026 under a Missouri statute for childhood sexual abuse claims. As of September 30, 2026, the date of the latest docket entry (re-checked 2026-10-05), the case and Sam Altman's defamation countersuit were active, a defense motion to dismiss (Doc. 109) was pending, and a December 2025 order had set a jury trial for May 3, 2027.
claims.passage: the judge dismissed her common-law claims as time-barred and allowed an amended complaint
claims.inference: Current procedural posture, stated neutrally with dates.
claims.alternative: Procedural rulings are not findings on the merits. The trial date comes from a December 2025 order and was not restated in later scheduling orders.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check the docket (courtlistener 69520118) immediately before release and at each refresh: the ruling on the defense motion to dismiss (Doc. 109), the Nov 16, 2026 dispositive-motion deadline and the May 3, 2027 trial date; restate the 'as of' date to match the check; update immediately on dismissal, settlement or verdict. Keep sanction, discovery and medical details out of copy.

claims.claim: In a January 2022 Art of Accomplishment episode Altman said: 'I think I started off my career in life as a very anxious, high-strung person, much more than I realized.'
claims.passage: a very anxious, high-strung person, much more than I realized
claims.inference: Anxiety behind a calm exterior fits Type 6 and is common in Threes whose worth rides on performance; the draft weighs it with the prepper record (C135-C137).
claims.alternative: The published page's 'I would wake up in the middle of the night with my heart pounding, just terrified' is unsourced (only in an anonymous Medium compilation, S99) and must be removed. Use 'no self that I can still find to identify with'. 'Crippling Anxiety' is the episode title, not his words.

claims.claim: In May 2024 Jan Leike, who led OpenAI's superalignment work on long-term AI risk, quit, posting: 'But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.' OpenAI disbanded the team.
claims.passage: safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products
claims.inference: Documented criticism from inside and outside OpenAI about the safety-versus-product trade-off under Altman.
claims.alternative: Organizational outcomes have many authors; Leike's criticism is aimed at OpenAI's leadership and priorities, not Altman by name.

claims.claim: On September 12, 2026 Altman posted: 'I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier', adding that committing to independent evaluators with employee-like access 'is a great idea, and we will do the same.'
claims.passage: I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier
claims.inference: A specific safety commitment that follows his general May 2024 reply to Leike (C139). The draft names the test (whether outside evaluators actually work inside OpenAI), unsettled as of 2026-10-05, and says it tests follow-through, not type.
claims.alternative: A commitment announced while OpenAI pursued an IPO path (S67, S95) could be partly reputational; a Three can also recalibrate sincerely.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check by 2027-03-12 (six months after the commitment) whether any outside evaluator has employee-like access at OpenAI, whether or not OpenAI has announced anything; also re-check when OpenAI announces embedded evaluators, files a public S-1 or sets an IPO date.

claims.claim: On February 2, 2026 Altman posted that after building an app with Codex, 'at least a couple of' its feature ideas 'were better than I was thinking of. I felt a little useless and it was sad.' He added: 'I am sure we will figure out much better and more interesting ways to spend our time, and amazing new ways to be useful to each other, but I am feeling nostalgic for the present.'
claims.passage: I felt a little useless and it was sad.
claims.inference: He names sadness at being outperformed, and at losing usefulness and competence. Feeling useless when no longer the best contributor fits a 3's worth-through-performance as well as a 4's wistfulness ('nostalgic for the present').
claims.alternative: He frames it as going 'off-script', a self-aware public post by the CEO selling the tool, so it doubles as marketing. Quote the post, not Fortune's altered version.

claims.claim: A Four reading hears wistfulness in the February 2026 Codex post; a Three reading hears the sting of being outdone, by a product he sells, at something he was good at, and a choice to say so in public. Both fit.
claims.passage: A Three reading hears the sting of being outdone
claims.inference: Presents the post as consistent with both leading hypotheses rather than as a discriminator.
claims.alternative: He framed the post as going 'off-script'; as CEO of the company selling the tool, it doubles as marketing.

claims.claim: Graham's prediction held, though by The New Yorker's account Graham's own YC was a place where partners stopped trusting him; Altman's 2026 apology describes the price of the same gift: rooms kept happy, fights put off, trust spent later. Whether he can lose a room on purpose is the forward test.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 3. (1) At about 17 he chose a costly public self-disclosure and challenged the school in front of everyone (C07, C82, C106): open confrontation that approval-seeking and the conflict-averse thesis do not predict, though he was already 'mostly out' and it was well received. (2) He voices feeling, sometimes privately and in real time: the 2023 email telling Musk 'it really fucking hurts' (C51), 'supermad' and 'This is just so fucked up' in November 2023 (C37, C39), 'Melancholy is a better word than sad' (C61), 'chaotic and shameful and upsetting' (C36), 'nostalgic for the present' (C62). (3) He has disclaimed status markers: $76,001 pay and no direct equity (C28), and 'I weirdly have very little personal ambition' (C30), which may reflect sincere mission. (4) In 2016 he called the 'missing circuit ... that would make me care what people think about me' 'a real gift' in the context of risk-taking (C22, C132), a direct denial of the approval motive, only partly qualified in 2019 (C86). (5) Power and control behavior supports Type 8: 'Only if the whole board quits' (C37), holding the line against Musk and 'Sam stood his ground' (C89, C90), 'I care more about power' (C31), the Samurai line (C02), Graham's 'extremely good at becoming powerful' (C12) and Friend's 'quick to anger' (C134). (6) Much of the accommodation and deception testimony is anonymous, adversarial, compilation-only, or from parties to the 2023 firing (C40, C46, C119, C16, C126); OpenAI disputes some of it (C121, C47) and WilmerHale found his conduct did not mandate removal (C50). His biographer frames the pattern as 'a typical critique of people who have the salesman skill set' (C42), and the record cannot separate craft from motive (C125). (7) Accommodation and wanting to be liked also fit Type 9 and Type 2 (C39, C40, C44, C34). Positive reframing ('outpouring of love', C33) and a biography titled The Optimist fit Seven-flavored optimism. The anxious strand and prepper record fit Six (C59, C135-C137).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4, the previously published reading (4w3), remains the strongest rival. It explains what Three cannot: the costly speech and public challenge at 17 (C07, C82, C106) and the private, unguarded hurt in the 2023 Musk email (C51). It also draws on 'melancholy' (C61), 'shameful' as one item in a list (C36), 'nostalgic for the present' (C62) and ambivalence about equity (C28). A reserved Four, or a Four with a strong Three wing, holds suffering in and could present as a polished public CEO (C99). Type 8 is the serious second alternative. It explains the power-seeking (C12, C31, C02), the hard control demands under threat (C37), refusing Musk's control (C89, C90) and Friend's 'quick to anger' (C134). It fails the accommodation test, and when Altman moves against people he does it indirectly (C120, C119, C100), whereas an Eight tends to fight in the open; Four outranks Eight for that reason (C133). Type 9 (conflict avoidance, 'unifying force'; C39, C41) and Type 2 (wanting to be liked, attentiveness; C40, C44, C34) explain the accommodation but not an agenda that survives every room (C105, C126, C127). Type 7 is suggested by upbeat reframing (C33) but not by years of fighting for one title or by the loss of usefulness he named (C128). Type 6 fits the anxiety and prepper record (C59, C135-C137) and is the largest residual (C138).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What his costly, repeated choices and his managed public face protect. A core 4 typically protects authentic self-expression even when it costs approval; a core 3 adjusts the presented self to win each room and, where looking credible and looking distinctive diverge, chooses credible. Across Loopt, YC and OpenAI (2005-2026), independent and adversarial sources describe accommodation in the room (C75, C42, C43, C44, C16) and indirect pursuit of his own aims outside it (C126, C120, C119); his own 'conflict-averse' label is treated as framing offered under accusation, not as corroboration (C124). The accommodation keeps his agenda (C105, C126, C127), which separates 3 from 9 (merging that dissolves its own agenda) and 2 (attentiveness that seeks to be needed). The focus on the top title (C45, C76, C129, C130) and the usefulness he mourned when outdone (C128) separate 3 from 7. Indirect sidelining while keeping the public face clean, rather than open fighting, separates 3 from 8 (C100, C120). Where credibility and distinctiveness pull apart, he chooses credibility (C78, C144, C54, C28). The edited argument deliberately does not use feeling-timing or the low-EQ self-reports as discriminators: a public record over-represents after-the-fact disclosure, his anger is sometimes immediate (C131), and the EQ quotes concern reading others (C19, C20, C108).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The costly speech and public challenge at 17 (C07, C106). The private, unguarded hurt in the 2023 Musk email (C51). The 2016 'missing circuit' denial of caring what people think, framed around risk (C22, C132), only partly qualified in 2019 (C86). The anxious strand and prepper record, which fit Type 6 as well as anything (C59, C135-C137). How much of the accommodation is a salesman's learned craft rather than core motive (C42, C125). Whether 'very little personal ambition' describes a sincere mission drive (C30). Whether his claimed change ('very happy to fire people quickly', C88) is real. The wing (3w4 vs 3w2) is not settled and is not asserted. The Annie Altman allegations (C69, C91) are unresolved and are not type evidence in either direction.
